options: Key people have concerns that the organization's business and IT systems are supposed to address
Tool vendors need a uniform format for exchanging models with each other
Operations teams need a complete inventory of the servers and licences that the organization owns
Developers need a detailed specification of classes and operations before starting work
explanation: An architecture is typically created because key people – stakeholders – have concerns that the organization's business and IT systems are supposed to address. The architect identifies these concerns and shows how they will be met. Exchanging models between tools, asset inventories and detailed software design are not reasons for creating an enterprise architecture.

question: Three hospitals and two health insurers, each with a different owner, are jointly building a shared platform for exchanging medical documentation. Can this grouping be regarded as an enterprise for the purposes of enterprise architecture?
options: Yes, an enterprise is any group of organizations with a common set of goals, e.g. a consortium
Yes, but only after the organizations merge into a single legal entity with common management
No, an enterprise consists of organizations linked by common ownership, which is not satisfied here
No, an enterprise is a whole corporation or its division, not a grouping of several independent entities
explanation: According to the definition adopted from the TOGAF standard, an enterprise is any group of organizations that have a common set of goals. It can be a whole corporation or a division of it, a government agency or a department of it, a chain of organizations linked by common ownership, but also partnerships and alliances, for example a consortium or a supply chain. Common ownership and a single legal entity are not prerequisites.

question: How does the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 standard, on which the explanation of the basic concepts is based, define architecture?
options: The fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment, embodied in its elements, relationships, and in the principles of its design and evolution
A complete inventory of all system components and their interfaces, organized by the technologies used in its implementation and operation
A formal description of an information system that can be used to procure products and develop its individual subsystems
The process of translating a business vision and strategy into change for the enterprise by means of principles and models of its future state
explanation: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 understands architecture as the fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment, embodied in its elements, relationships, and in the principles of its design and evolution. A formal description of a system serving as a blueprint for procurement and development is an architecture description, not the architecture itself. A process of translating a vision and strategy into change is one of the conceptions of Enterprise Architecture.

question: The explanation of the basic concepts presents two conceptions of Enterprise Architecture. Which pair captures them?
options: A process translating a business vision and strategy into effective enterprise change; a set of abstractions and models that simplify complex structures
The fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment; a specification of conventions for a certain kind of views of the architecture
A formal description of an information system serving as a blueprint for procuring products; a representation of a system from the perspective of certain concerns
A process of managing projects and change programmes across the whole organization; a set of plans and schedules used to track these projects
explanation: The first conception (Gartner) understands Enterprise Architecture as a process that translates a business vision and strategy into effective enterprise change by creating, communicating and improving the key principles and models that describe the future state. The second (DoDAF) understands it as a set of abstractions and models that simplify and communicate complex structures, processes, rules and constraints. The fundamental concepts or properties of a system are the definition of architecture according to ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, a formal description of a system is an architecture description, and the remaining formulations delimit view and viewpoint.

question: A team of developers will maintain a new system, but it does not decide on its procurement and does not fund it. Is it among the stakeholders of the system?
options: Yes, a stakeholder is anyone who has a key role in the system or has concerns about it
Yes, provided that it is drawn in the model as a Business Actor with its own business role
No, stakeholders are those who fund the system or approve its procurement and operation
No, a stakeholder can be an individual or a whole organization, not a work team
explanation: Stakeholders are people who have a key role in the system or have concerns about it – for example users or developers – and they can be individuals, teams or whole organizations. Decision-making authority and funding are not prerequisites. Whether someone is a stakeholder also does not depend on how they are drawn in the model.

question: What are concerns in enterprise architecture?
options: Key interests of stakeholders that determine the acceptability of the system, e.g. performance or security
Formal requirements on the system that the architect records as a Requirement, e.g. response time or availability
Identified differences between two states of the architecture that the architect records as a Gap, e.g. a missing interface
Risks of the system implementation project tracked by the project manager, e.g. delays or budget overruns
explanation: Concerns are key interests that are crucially important to stakeholders and determine the acceptability of the system; they can relate, for example, to performance, reliability, security, distribution or evolvability. A Requirement is a refined need that the architect derives from concerns, and a Gap describes the difference between two plateaus.

question:
Which two of the following statements about how an architect addresses stakeholders' concerns are true?
1. The architect identifies stakeholders' requirements and further refines them.
2. The architect addresses the concerns of the most senior stakeholder and leaves out the concerns of the others from the architecture.
3. The architect shows what trade-offs are required to reconcile the concerns of different stakeholders, which may conflict.
4. The architect does not create views, because the way of addressing concerns is determined only during implementation.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
explanation: The architect addresses concerns by identifying and refining stakeholders' requirements, by creating views that show how the concerns and requirements will be met, and by showing the trade-offs required to reconcile the potentially conflicting concerns of different stakeholders. The architect therefore does not leave out the concerns of less important stakeholders, and views are the main tool. Without an architecture, it would be hard to consider and meet all concerns and requirements.

question: What are architecture descriptions used for?
options: They formally describe an information system so that it is possible to reason about its structural and behavioural properties and about its evolution
They informally summarize stakeholders' wishes so that priorities can be decided before architecture work begins
They formally describe the course of a single project so that its budget, deadlines and delivered outputs can be tracked
They formally describe the notation of a modelling language so that a tool's conformance with the requirements of the standard can be verified
explanation: Architecture descriptions are formal descriptions of an information system, organized in such a way as to support reasoning about its structural and behavioural properties and about its evolution. They define the components or building blocks of the system and provide a blueprint from which products can be procured and subsystems developed that will work together. They are neither a project plan nor an informal wish list.

question: An architect is explaining to hospital management how the Business, Application and Technology layers differ and how they are related in the model. Which explanation corresponds to the ArchiMate language?
options: The layers provide services to each other (service-orientation); realization leads from concrete elements to more abstract ones across layers
The layers provide services to each other (service-orientation); specialization leads from concrete elements to more abstract ones across layers
The layers inherit properties from each other (object-orientation); realization leads from concrete elements to more abstract ones across layers
The layers inherit properties from each other (object-orientation); specialization leads from concrete elements to more abstract ones across layers
explanation: ArchiMate distinguishes the Business, Application and Technology layers and at the same time connects them by service-orientation – the layers provide services to each other. By the realization relationship, it then connects, across layers, more concrete elements with the more abstract ones that they help to bring about, for example a Data Object with a Business Object. Specialization expresses a relationship between a more general and a more specific kind of the same element type, not a link across layers.

image.alt: Example of cross-layer alignment: technology service serves application component, application service serves business process, data object realizes business object, and artifacts realize data object and application component.

question: What does it mean that ArchiMate offers an integrated architecture approach?
options: A single language covers several architecture domains, including the links and dependencies between them
It combines a modelling language with a method that prescribes the individual phases of enterprise architecture development
It merges the UML, BPMN and ERD notations into a single diagram for every stakeholder
It connects models with project management tools and system configuration management tools
explanation: An integrated architecture approach means that one language describes and visualizes various architecture domains as well as the relationships and dependencies between them. ArchiMate is not a method – a phased procedure for developing an architecture is provided, for example, by the TOGAF ADM – and it neither replaces nor merges detailed languages such as UML or BPMN.

question: An insurance company wants to record its own attributes for model elements and show management views tailored to its concerns. Is the ArchiMate language sufficient for this?
options: Yes, the language includes viewpoints for selected stakeholders and mechanisms for its customization
Yes, the language prescribes a phased procedure for developing an architecture and templates for its outputs
No, the language has a single fixed notation and its elements cannot be supplemented with additional properties
No, the language describes relationships between layers and leaves views for stakeholders to UML
explanation: In addition to a uniform representation of diagrams and concepts for interrelated architectures, the ArchiMate language includes specific viewpoints for selected stakeholders and mechanisms for customizing the language, which can be used, for example, to add custom attributes. It does not prescribe a phased procedure for architecture work – that is addressed by frameworks such as TOGAF – and it separates notation from concepts, so the depiction can be adapted to stakeholders.

question: How does the ArchiMate specification define an aspect?
options: A classification of elements based on layer-independent characteristics related to the concerns of different stakeholders
A level of abstraction of the ArchiMate framework at which an enterprise can be modelled, for example Business or Technology
A property associated with an element or relationship of the language, for example cost or criticality given in a profile
A specification of conventions for a certain kind of view of the architecture, intended for selected stakeholders
explanation: An aspect is a classification of elements based on characteristics that are independent of the layer and related to the concerns of different stakeholders; it is used to position elements in the metamodel (active structure, behavior, passive structure, and in the full framework also motivation). The level of abstraction at which an enterprise can be modelled is, by contrast, the layer. A property of an element or relationship is an attribute, and the conventions for a certain kind of view are determined by a viewpoint.

question: What is the relationship between the terms ArchiMate core language and ArchiMate Core Framework?
options: The core language is the central part of the language with the concepts of three layers; the Core Framework is a reference structure that classifies its elements
The core language is the standard notation of the elements of three layers; the Core Framework is a metamodel that determines the permitted relationships between them
The Core Framework is the central part of the language with the concepts of three layers; the core language is a reference structure that classifies its elements
The core language and the Core Framework both denote the same thing: the matrix of layers and aspects of the full language including the Motivation aspect
explanation: The core language is the central part of the language, defining the concepts for modelling enterprise architectures from three layers: Business, Application and Technology (including physical elements). The Core Framework is a reference structure of three layers and three aspects by which the elements of the core language are classified. The permitted relationships are determined by the metamodel, not by the framework, and the Motivation aspect, together with the Strategy and Implementation and Migration layers, is added only by the Full Framework.

image.alt: Table of the ArchiMate Core Framework: three layers (Business, Application, Technology) and three aspects (Passive structure, Behavior, Active structure) with examples of elements.

question: What is an attribute according to the definitions in the ArchiMate specification?
options: A property associated with an element or relationship of the language
A property associated with an element, but not with a relationship
An icon associated with an element in the standard notation of the language
A cell of the framework into which an element of the language is classified
explanation: An attribute is a property associated with an element or relationship of the ArchiMate language – attributes can therefore be carried by elements as well as relationships, for example by means of profiles. An icon is part of the notation, and classification into a layer and aspect is a classification according to the framework, not an attribute.

question: How are the terms conformance and conforming implementation defined in the ArchiMate specification?
options: Conformance is the fulfilment of specified requirements; a conforming implementation satisfies the requirements of the standard's conformance clause
Conformance is the agreement of a model with a viewpoint; a conforming implementation is a view created according to the rules of this viewpoint
Conformance is the certification of an individual; a conforming implementation is training accredited for the given certification level
Conformance is the validity of a derived relationship; a conforming implementation is a model that contains only valid derivations
explanation: Conformance is, in general, the fulfilment of specified requirements. A conforming implementation is an implementation (typically a modelling tool) that satisfies the conformance requirements defined in the conformance clause of the standard. It is not about the certification of persons or about the relationship between a view and a viewpoint.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the ArchiMate certification programme are true?
1. The certification is intended for individuals who want to demonstrate knowledge of the language according to the ArchiMate 3.x Specification or its subsequent minor releases.
2. The Foundation level is obtained by passing the ArchiMate 3 Part 1 exam, a simple multiple-choice test with 40 questions.
3. The learning outcomes of the Foundation level focus on application and analysis.
4. The programme is tied to version 3.0 and is not expected to evolve with further versions of the language.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
explanation: The certification is intended for individuals and is tied to the ArchiMate 3.x Specification and its subsequent minor releases; the programme is expected to evolve further with new versions of the language. Foundation verifies knowledge and understanding of the notation, terminology, structure and basic concepts and is obtained by the Part 1 exam with 40 multiple-choice questions. Application and analysis are the focus only of the Practitioner level.

question: Which term does the specification define as the basic unit of the ArchiMate metamodel, used to define and describe the parts of enterprise architectures and their unique characteristics?
options: Element
Concept
Attribute
Model
explanation: An element is the basic unit of the ArchiMate metamodel, used to define and describe the individual parts of enterprise architectures and their unique characteristics. A concept is a broader term – it includes elements and relationships – a model is a collection of concepts and an attribute is a property associated with an element or relationship.

image.alt: Tree of the ArchiMate concept hierarchy: a model consists of concepts, a concept is an element, relationship or relationship connector, an element is divided into behavior, structure (active/passive), motivation and composite.

question: Into which four kinds is an element divided in the top-level concept hierarchy?
options: Behavior, structure, motivation and composite element
Business, application, technology and physical element
Active structure, behavior, passive structure and motivation element
Core, strategy, motivation and implementation element
explanation: In the top-level hierarchy, a model is a collection of concepts and a concept is an element, relationship or relationship connector. An element is further divided into behavior element, structure element, motivation element and composite element. Active structure, behavior, passive structure and motivation are aspects of the framework and Business, Application and Technology are its layers – that is a different classification.

image.alt: Tree of the ArchiMate concept hierarchy: a model consists of concepts, a concept is an element, relationship or relationship connector, an element is divided into behavior, structure (active/passive), motivation and composite.

question: Complete: In the generic metamodel, the realization relationship is drawn from … to the external behavior element (service).
options: internal behavior element
internal active structure element
external active structure element
passive structure element
explanation: In the generic metamodel, the realization relationship leads from the internal behavior element to the service: internal behaviour (e.g. a process or function) brings the service about. An internal active structure element is assigned to this behaviour (assignment) and an interface, i.e. an external active structure element, is assigned to the service that it exposes. That, for example, a component realizes a service can be obtained only by derivation via internal behaviour.

image.alt: ArchiMate generic metamodel: internal and external active structure, internal behavior, service, event and passive structure with the relationships assigned to, realizes, serves, accesses, triggers/flows to and composed of.

question: Which relationship leads in the generic metamodel from the internal active structure element to the event element?
options: Assignment
Access
Realization
Composition
explanation: In the generic metamodel, the internal active structure element is connected by an assignment relationship not only to the internal behavior element, but also to the event element – active structure can thus be the originator of an event. Access points to passive structure elements, realization leads from internal behaviour to a service, and composition in the metamodel connects an internal active structure element with its interface, not with an event.

image.alt: ArchiMate generic metamodel: internal and external active structure, internal behavior, service, event and passive structure with the relationships assigned to, realizes, serves, accesses, triggers/flows to and composed of.

question: Which of the behaviour elements have an access relationship to a passive structure element drawn in the generic metamodel?
options: Internal behavior element, service and event
Internal behavior element and service, but not event
Internal behavior element and event, but not service
Internal behavior element, but neither service nor event
explanation: In the generic metamodel, the access relationship to a passive structure element leads from all three kinds of behaviour elements: from the internal behavior element, from a service (external behavior element) and from the event element. Behaviour can thus read, create or modify passive structure regardless of whether it is internal behaviour, a service or an event.

image.alt: ArchiMate generic metamodel: internal and external active structure, internal behavior, service, event and passive structure with the relationships assigned to, realizes, serves, accesses, triggers/flows to and composed of.

question: How does the generic metamodel define an internal behavior element?
options: A unit of activity that can be performed by one or more active structure elements
Explicitly defined behaviour that is exposed to the environment of the given element
A unit of collective behaviour performed by at least two elements
A state change that can trigger other behaviour or be triggered by it
explanation: An internal behavior element is a unit of activity that can be performed by one or more active structure elements; its specializations are process, function and interaction. Explicitly defined behaviour exposed to the environment is a service (external behavior element), collective behaviour of at least two elements is an interaction, and a state change is represented by an event.

question: Where does the generic metamodel place the event element?
options: Among behavior elements, alongside the internal behavior element and the service
Among relationship connectors, alongside the junction for triggering relationships
Among passive structure elements, alongside the objects that behaviour accesses
Among composite elements, alongside the grouping and location elements
explanation: In the generic metamodel, an event is a behaviour element: it represents a state change, can trigger behaviour (triggering) or be triggered by it, and an active structure element can be assigned to it. It is not a relationship connector – that is the junction – nor a passive structure element or a composite element.

image.alt: ArchiMate generic metamodel: internal and external active structure, internal behavior, service, event and passive structure with the relationships assigned to, realizes, serves, accesses, triggers/flows to and composed of.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the classification of elements into the aspects of the ArchiMate Full Framework are true?
1. Contract belongs to the behavior aspect.
2. System Software belongs to the active structure aspect.
3. Assessment belongs to the passive structure aspect.
4. Value Stream belongs to the behavior aspect.
options: 2 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
3 and 4
explanation: System Software is an active structure element of the Technology Layer and Value Stream is a behaviour element of the Strategy layer. Contract is a specialization of Business Object, so it belongs to the passive structure aspect, and Assessment is a motivation element, so it falls into the motivation aspect.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the Location element are true?
1. It may aggregate only active structure elements, for example actors and devices.
2. It is a specialization of the Facility element from the Technology Layer.
3. It can represent a conceptual as well as a physical place or position.
4. It expresses where structure elements are located or where behaviour is performed.
options: 3 and 4
1 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 2
explanation: A Location represents a conceptual or physical place or position where concepts are located (e.g. structure elements) or where they are performed (e.g. behaviour elements). It is a composite element that aggregates these concepts – it is not a specialization of the Facility element and is not limited to active structure.

question: A diagram contains the Grouping "Payment Core", inside which two application functions and one data object are drawn; a realization relationship leads from the Grouping to the application service "Payment Processing". How should this notation be read?
options: The Grouping aggregates or composes the nested concepts and the group as a whole realizes the service
The Grouping is a graphical frame outside the model, so the relationship leading to the service is invalid
The Grouping is an active structure element that performs the functions and provides the service to the environment
The Grouping is a specialization of an application function, so it realizes the service in the same way as a function
explanation: A Grouping aggregates or composes concepts that belong together on the basis of a shared characteristic; nesting is only an alternative notation of these aggregation or composition relationships. A group is a full-fledged model element, so a relationship can lead from it to another element – here the functions and the data object together realize the service. A Grouping is neither active structure nor a specialization of a function.

question: The ArchiMate aspects are based on natural language: the subject corresponds to active structure, the verb to behavior and the object to passive structure. Does the order of these aspects matter for the placement of elements in a diagram?
options: No, ArchiMate is a graphical language, elements are arranged spatially and the order of the aspects plays no role
Yes, elements are arranged from left to right in the order passive structure, behavior and active structure
Yes, active structure is drawn at the top, behavior in the middle and passive structure at the bottom
No, the order is determined by the viewpoint, which prescribes its own arrangement of aspects for each view
explanation: The aspects are based on the sentence structure of natural language, but ArchiMate is a graphical language in which elements are arranged spatially. The order subject – verb – object therefore has no meaning for modelling, and neither the framework, the aspects nor a viewpoint prescribe the placement of elements in a diagram.

question: In one view, a Business Process is drawn as a box with an arrow icon in the corner, in another view as the arrow symbol alone. What does this mean for the model?
options: These are two notations of the same concept; in the model it is still the same element type
These are two different element types; the box denotes a process and the arrow symbol triggering
It is a notation error; the standard permits a single notation for each concept
It is a specialization; the arrow symbol denotes a subtype defined in a profile
explanation: ArchiMate separates the concepts of the language from their notation, so the same concept can be displayed in different ways – for example as a box with an icon in the corner or as the symbol alone. This changes nothing in the model: in both views it is a Business Process. Different notations make it possible to adapt the depiction to different groups of stakeholders.

image.alt: ArchiMate notation cues: corner shape by aspect, optional layer letter in the top left corner, an element written as a box with an icon or as an icon only, Grouping and Location.

question: Nesting is an alternative graphical notation for only some relationships. Which of the following relationships can NOT be expressed by nesting?
options: Triggering
Composition
Aggregation
Assignment
explanation: Only some relationships can be alternatively written by nesting, typically structural ones – for example composition, aggregation or assignment, where one element is drawn inside another. Triggering is a dynamic relationship expressing temporal or causal sequence between elements and is drawn with an arrow; it cannot be expressed by nesting.

image.alt: The same model drawn twice: with composition and assignment lines and using nesting of elements.

question: What does a white box fill denote in the metamodel figures of the ArchiMate specification?
options: An abstract concept that cannot be instantiated in a model
A passive structure element on which behaviour is performed
An element that does not belong to any of the layers of the core language
An optional concept that a tool does not have to support
explanation: In the metamodel figures, shades of grey distinguish the aspects and a white fill denotes abstract, i.e. non-instantiable, concepts (e.g. the internal behavior element). Passive structure is light grey, behaviour medium grey and active structure dark grey. This convention has nothing to do with tool support or with layers.

question: In the metamodel figures of the ArchiMate specification, shades of grey distinguish the aspects. What fill do the boxes of the elements Business Object, Business Process and Business Actor have there (in this order)?
options: Light grey, medium grey and dark grey
Dark grey, medium grey and light grey
Medium grey, light grey and dark grey
Light grey, dark grey and medium grey
explanation: In the metamodel figures, light grey denotes passive structure (Business Object), medium grey behaviour (Business Process) and dark grey active structure (Business Actor); white is reserved for abstract concepts. This is a convention of the metamodel figures – in the models themselves, colours have no formal meaning.

question: In many example models in the ArchiMate standard, colours are used to distinguish the layers of the Core Framework, even though they have no formal meaning. Which combination corresponds to this custom?
options: Yellow – Business Layer, blue – Application Layer, green – Technology Layer
Blue – Business Layer, green – Application Layer, yellow – Technology Layer
Green – Business Layer, yellow – Application Layer, blue – Technology Layer
Yellow – Business Layer, green – Application Layer, blue – Technology Layer
explanation: Colours have no formal semantics in ArchiMate models and their use is left to the modeller, for example for visually emphasizing a part of the model. In many examples in the standard, however, the layers of the Core Framework are distinguished by colour: yellow for the Business Layer, blue for the Application Layer and green for the Technology Layer. This is a custom, not a rule of the language.

image.alt: Table of the ArchiMate Core Framework: three layers (Business, Application, Technology) and three aspects (Passive structure, Behavior, Active structure) with examples of elements.

question: An element has the letter "P" in the top left corner. What does this notation cue denote?
options: A physical element (Physical)
A passive structure element (Passive structure)
A process-type element (Process)
A product-type element (Product)
explanation: The letter in the top left corner of an element denotes the layer or area of the language: M = Motivation, S = Strategy, B = Business, A = Application, T = Technology, P = Physical and I = Implementation & Migration. "P" therefore denotes a physical element, for example Equipment or Facility. Aspects and individual element types are not denoted by letters.

image.alt: ArchiMate notation cues: corner shape by aspect, optional layer letter in the top left corner, an element written as a box with an icon or as an icon only, Grouping and Location.

question: Which assignment of a letter in the top left corner to an element corresponds to the ArchiMate notation cues?
options: The letter "I" for the Deliverable element
The letter "S" for the Stakeholder element
The letter "B" for the Capability element
The letter "P" for the Plateau element
explanation: A Deliverable belongs to the Implementation & Migration layer, which is denoted by the letter "I". A Stakeholder is a motivation element (letter "M"), a Capability is an element of the Strategy layer ("S") and a Plateau also belongs to Implementation & Migration ("I"). The letter therefore does not follow the initial letter of the element's name, but where the element belongs in the language.

image.alt: ArchiMate notation cues: corner shape by aspect, optional layer letter in the top left corner, an element written as a box with an icon or as an icon only, Grouping and Location.

question: Which pair of elements is drawn in the standard notation as boxes with rounded corners?
options: Business Process and Application Service
Business Actor and Application Component
Business Object and Technology Service
Requirement and Business Function
explanation: Rounded corners are in the standard notation a mark of behaviour elements, which include both Business Process and Application Service. Structure elements (Business Actor, Application Component, Business Object) have square corners and motivation elements, for example Requirement, bevelled corners.

image.alt: ArchiMate notation cues: corner shape by aspect, optional layer letter in the top left corner, an element written as a box with an icon or as an icon only, Grouping and Location.

question: How is the Grouping element drawn in the standard ArchiMate notation?
options: As a box with a dashed outline, possibly with a tab at the top like a folder
As a box with a solid outline and a double line along the top edge
As a box with bevelled corners and a folder icon in the top right corner
As an oval with a dotted outline around the grouped elements of the diagram
explanation: A Grouping is drawn as a rectangle with a dashed outline; in an alternative form it has a tab at the top, like a folder. Bevelled corners are a mark of motivation elements, and a solid outline with a stripe along the top edge is used by passive structure elements, for example Business Object.

image.alt: ArchiMate notation cues: corner shape by aspect, optional layer letter in the top left corner, an element written as a box with an icon or as an icon only, Grouping and Location.

question: How is the Location element recognised in the standard notation?
options: By the pin icon, as used to mark a place on a map
By the icon of a factory building with a sawtooth roof
By the dashed outline of a box with a tab at the top
By the icon of a three-dimensional box in the corner of the box
explanation: A Location is denoted by the icon of a pin (a place marker on a map) in the top right corner of the box, or by this symbol alone. A Facility has the factory icon, a Grouping the dashed outline and a Node the three-dimensional box.

image.alt: ArchiMate notation cues: corner shape by aspect, optional layer letter in the top left corner, an element written as a box with an icon or as an icon only, Grouping and Location.

question: What do dependency relationships generally model according to ArchiMate?
options: How some elements are used to support other elements
How concepts are statically arranged and what they are composed of
How behaviour elements follow one another in time or causally
That an element is a special kind of another element of the same type
explanation: Dependency relationships (serving, access, influence and association) describe how elements support other elements and are used by them. The static structure and composition of concepts are modelled by structural relationships and the sequencing of behaviour by dynamic relationships. "A special kind of another element" is expressed by specialization from the category of other relationships.

image.alt: Overview of the notation of all ArchiMate relationships, divided into structural, dependency, dynamic and other, including the AND and OR junctions.

question: Which of the following pairs of relationships belong to the same category in ArchiMate 3.2?
options: Triggering and flow
Realization and specialization
Access and flow
Assignment and serving
explanation: Triggering and flow are both dynamic relationships. Realization is a structural relationship, whereas specialization belongs to the category other, even though both are drawn with a hollow triangle. Access and serving are dependency relationships, whereas flow is dynamic and assignment structural.

image.alt: Overview of the notation of all ArchiMate relationships, divided into structural, dependency, dynamic and other, including the AND and OR junctions.

question: Complete: The category of other relationships in ArchiMate 3.2 consists of ___.
options: a single relationship, namely specialization
two relationships, specialization and association
two relationships, association and influence
the specialization relationship and the junction connector
explanation: The category of other relationships in ArchiMate 3.2 contains a single relationship – specialization. Association and influence are dependency relationships. A junction is not a relationship but a relationship connector, and so it stands outside all four categories of relationships.

image.alt: Overview of the notation of all ArchiMate relationships, divided into structural, dependency, dynamic and other, including the AND and OR junctions.

question: What can be an endpoint of a relationship, i.e. its source or target, according to ArchiMate 3.2?
options: An element, another relationship or a relationship connector
An element or another relationship, but not a relationship connector
An element or a relationship connector, but not another relationship
A core element or a composite element, but not a relationship or a connector
explanation: Every relationship has exactly one source and exactly one target, and this endpoint can be an element, another relationship or a relationship connector (junction). Further restrictions apply, however: for example, two relationships cannot be connected to each other, and an element is connected to another relationship typically by an association relationship.

question: The Business Function "Receivables Management" realizes the Business Service "Debt Collection" (realization leads from the function to the service). What is the usual interpretation of such a relationship?
options: The function (whole or a part of it) realizes the whole service
The function (whole or a part of it) realizes some part of the service
The service (whole or a part of it) realizes the whole function
The service (whole or a part of it) realizes some part of the function
explanation: The usual interpretation of realization is that the source element as a whole, or some part of it, realizes the whole target element. The source here is the function and the target the service, so reading it as "the service realizes the function" is reversed. Realization of merely a part of the service does not correspond to this interpretation – the target element is realized as a whole.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the realization relationship are true?
1. The triangle at the end of the line points to the more concrete ("physical") element.
2. It is used to model run-time realization.
3. The realized element expresses the "what" (logical level), the realizing element the "how" (physical level).
4. It may connect only elements of the same layer.
options: 2 and 3
1 and 2
3 and 4
1 and 4
explanation: Realization says that a more abstract element (the "what", logical) is realized by a more tangible element (the "how", physical), and it is used for run-time realization. The relationship leads from the more concrete element to the more abstract one, so the triangle is at the more abstract element. Realization commonly also connects elements of different layers, e.g. it leads from a Data Object to a Business Object.

question: The Data Object "Address" is part (composition) of the Data Object "Client". The architect wants to include the same object "Address" in the Data Object "Supplier" as well, by another composition relationship. What does ArchiMate say about this?
options: It is not correct; the same concept may be part of only one composition
It is fine; composition is always permitted between elements of the same type
It is fine if both compositions are drawn by nesting elements
It is not correct; composition may lead only between elements of different types
explanation: A concept that is part of a composition can belong to only one composition; the same element can be included in several wholes by an aggregation relationship. The fact that composition is always permitted between two elements of the same type does not remove this restriction. Nesting is just another notation of the same relationship, so it changes nothing.

question: Which element is the source in composition and aggregation relationships, and how is the relationship read in the direction from source to target?
options: The source is the whole; it reads "composed of" and "aggregates" respectively
The source is the part; it reads "composed in" and "aggregated in" respectively
The source is the whole; it reads "composed in" and "aggregated in" respectively
The source is the part; it reads "composed of" and "aggregates" respectively
explanation: In both composition and aggregation, the source is the whole – the diamond is drawn at it – and the target is the part. From source to target, the relationship reads "composed of" and "aggregates" respectively; in the opposite direction, from the part to the whole, "composed in" and "aggregated in" respectively.

image.alt: Overview of the notation of all ArchiMate relationships, divided into structural, dependency, dynamic and other, including the AND and OR junctions.

question: According to the semantics of structural relationships, what holds for the element on the source side of the relationship?
options: It contains, groups, performs or realizes the concept on the target side
It is contained, grouped, performed or realized by the concept on the target side
It serves, reads, writes or influences the concept on the target side
It triggers the concept on the target side or passes information or goods to it
explanation: Structural relationships say that the element on the source side contains, groups, performs or realizes the concept on the target side: a whole contains a part, a role performs a process, a process realizes a service. The reversed reading swaps source and target. Serving, access and influence are dependency relationships, triggering and transfer are dynamic relationships.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the semantics of relationships are true?
1. Structural relationships can be applied transitively also to the (possibly unmodelled) parts of the source element.
2. A dependency relationship means that all parts of the target element depend on the source element.
3. In a specialization, the general element is specialized as a whole.
4. Flow follows the same semantics as structural relationships.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
explanation: Structural relationships can be applied transitively also to the (possibly unmodelled) parts of the source element, and in a specialization the general element is specialized as a whole by the specialized element. A dependency, on the contrary, need not hold for all parts of an element – it says only that a part of the target depends on a part of the source. Flow follows this semantics of dependencies; triggering corresponds to structural relationships.

question: The Application Service "Risk Calculation" serves the Business Process "Application Assessment" (serving leads from the service to the process). What follows from this according to the semantics of dependency relationships?
options: Some part of the process depends on some part of the service
Some part of the service depends on some part of the process
Every part of the process depends on the service as a whole
Every part of the service depends on the process as a whole
explanation: For dependency relationships, a part of the target element depends on a part of the source element. The target of the serving here is the process, so the process depends on the service, not the service on the process. The dependency need not concern all parts of an element, so it cannot be claimed that every subprocess depends on the service.

question: ArchiMate 3.2 distinguishes several kinds of dependency among dependency relationships. Which assignment is correct?
options: Serving – control, access – data, influence – impact dependency
Serving – data, access – control, influence – impact dependency
Serving – impact, access – data, influence – control dependency
Serving – control, access – impact, influence – data dependency
explanation: Serving represents a control dependency, access a data dependency and influence an impact dependency. The fourth relationship of this category, association, expresses a dependency that none of the other relationships covers.

question: For what situation is the association relationship suitable, apart from cases that no other relationship type covers?
options: For a first, rough model, where relationships are marked in general terms and refined later
For a detailed model, where it stands in for derived relationships between layers
For a target architecture, where it marks relationships that will only come into being
For a motivation model, where no other relationship type can be used
explanation: Association can be used when drawing a first, high-level model: relationships are drawn in general terms first and later replaced by more specific types. It is not a substitute for derived relationships nor a mark of a future state. In motivation models, realization, influence or aggregation are commonly used alongside it.

question: How is a directed association drawn in ArchiMate 3.2?
options: A solid line with half of an open arrowhead at the target
A solid line with a full open arrowhead at the target
A dashed line with an open arrowhead at the target
A solid line with a hollow triangle at the target
explanation: An undirected association is a plain solid line; the directed variant has only half of an open arrowhead at the target. A solid line with a full open arrowhead is serving, a dashed line with an open arrowhead belongs to the influence and access relationships, and a solid line with a hollow triangle is specialization.

image.alt: Variants of the Access relationship (no arrowhead, read, write, read-write), Influence with a plus and minus sign, and Association undirected and directed.

question: What kind of element does an influence relationship, by definition, point to, i.e. what is its target?
options: A motivation element, for example a goal or a principle
A behaviour element, for example a process or a function
A passive element, for example a data object or an artifact
An active element, for example a business actor or a node
explanation: Influence expresses that an element influences the implementation or achievement of some motivation element, for example a goal or a principle. The target of the relationship is therefore a motivation element; it can be influenced by another motivation element as well as by an element of the architecture. Sequencing in behaviour is modelled by dynamic relationships and work with passive elements by access.

image.alt: Variants of the Access relationship (no arrowhead, read, write, read-write), Influence with a plus and minus sign, and Association undirected and directed.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the influence relationship are true?
1. Without an attribute being given, the influence is considered positive.
2. The set of attribute values for the sign and strength of the influence is chosen by the modeller.
3. It belongs among the dynamic relationships.
4. Without an attribute being given, it is a contribution with an unspecified sign and strength.
options: 2 and 4
1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 3
explanation: The standard does not prescribe the values of the attribute that expresses the sign and strength of the influence – they are chosen by the modeller, e.g. {++, +, 0, −, −−} or a scale from 0 to 10. Without the attribute, the relationship means a contribution with an unspecified sign and strength, not automatically a positive influence. Influence belongs among the dependency relationships.

image.alt: Variants of the Access relationship (no arrowhead, read, write, read-write), Influence with a plus and minus sign, and Association undirected and directed.

question: The Requirement "Two-step verification" significantly helps the Goal "Higher security", but worsens the achievement of the goal "Convenient login". What is the best way to express this?
options: By two influence relationships from the requirement to the goals, with labels such as ++ and −
By two influence relationships from the goals to the requirement, with labels such as ++ and −
By two realization relationships from the requirement to the goals, with labels such as ++ and −
By two triggering relationships from the requirement to the goals, with labels such as ++ and −
explanation: Influence leads from the influencing element to the influenced motivation element; the sign and strength of the influence are expressed by an attribute displayed as a label, separately for each relationship. Realization would claim that the requirement plays a critical role in achieving both goals, and it cannot express a negative influence. Triggering is a dynamic relationship between behaviour elements.

image.alt: Variants of the Access relationship (no arrowhead, read, write, read-write), Influence with a plus and minus sign, and Association undirected and directed.

question: An access relationship between a Business Process and a Business Object is drawn with no arrowhead at either end. What does this mean?
options: It is valid; the kind of access to the object is left unspecified
It is valid; it means reading and writing the object at the same time
It is invalid; an access relationship has an arrowhead at least at one end
It is invalid; only an association may have a line without an arrowhead
explanation: The arrowhead on an access relationship is optional: when present, it expresses the creation, modification or use of the passive element. An access relationship without an arrowhead is valid and leaves the kind of access unspecified; it can also be used to say that the object merely relates to the behaviour element. Reading and writing at the same time is shown with arrowheads at both ends.

image.alt: Variants of the Access relationship (no arrowhead, read, write, read-write), Influence with a plus and a minus sign, and Association undirected and directed.

question: Which of the following elements CANNOT be the source of an access relationship?
options: Business Object
Business Service
Business Event
Business Role
explanation: Access expresses the ability of behaviour and active structure elements to observe passive structure elements or to do something with them. The source can therefore be a process, function, interaction, service or event, as well as an active structure element such as a role. A Business Object is itself a passive element: it does not perform anything and is the target of an access relationship.

question: Which statement about the use of the serving relationship is consistent with ArchiMate?
options: It is used in both the behaviour and the active structure aspect, e.g. service → process and interface → actor
It is used in the behaviour aspect, e.g. service → process, but not in the active structure aspect
It is used in the active structure aspect, e.g. interface → actor, but not in the behaviour aspect
It is used in both the behaviour and the passive structure aspect, e.g. service → process and object → actor
explanation: Serving describes how the services or interfaces of an element serve the entities in its environment, and it applies in the behaviour aspect (a service serves a process) as well as in the active structure aspect (an interface serves an actor or a role). A passive element provides no functionality, so it cannot be the source of serving.

question: Does ArchiMate distinguish, in the triggering relationship, between an active trigger and a passive causal connection?
options: No, triggering covers both and does not distinguish between them in any way
Yes, an active trigger has a filled arrowhead and a passive causal connection an open one
Yes, a passive causal connection is modelled with the flow relationship
No, triggering expresses an active trigger and causality cannot be modelled
explanation: Triggering expresses a temporal or causal succession, and ArchiMate does not distinguish whether it is an active trigger or a passive causal connection. Flow models a transfer and does not imply causality. A solid line with an open arrowhead is not a variant of triggering but the serving relationship.

question: The triggering and flow relationships both belong to the dynamic relationships. Which semantics does each follow according to ArchiMate?
options: Triggering follows the semantics of structural relationships, flow the semantics of dependency relationships
Triggering follows the semantics of dependency relationships, flow the semantics of structural relationships
Both follow the semantics of dependency relationships, i.e. the same as, for example, serving
Both follow the semantics of structural relationships, i.e. the same as, for example, assignment
explanation: The semantics of the two dynamic relationships differ: triggering follows the semantics of structural relationships, flow the semantics of dependency relationships. With flow, part of the target element therefore depends on part of the source element, similarly to serving.

question: A flow labelled “delivery note” runs between the Business Function “Purchasing” and the Business Function “Warehousing”. What does such a label on a flow relationship express?
options: What is transferred between the two functions
The condition under which the target function is triggered
The role responsible for the handover between the functions
The strength of the dependence of the target function on the source function
explanation: Flow expresses a transfer, for example of information, goods or money, between behaviour elements, and the label of the relationship names what is transferred. Flow itself does not imply a causal succession, so the label is not a triggering condition. Strength and sign are attributes of the influence relationship, not of flow.

question: The Business Role “Paediatrician” is a special kind of the role “Physician”. How is this drawn with the specialization relationship?
options: From the role “Paediatrician” to the role “Physician”; the triangle is at the role “Physician”
From the role “Physician” to the role “Paediatrician”; the triangle is at the role “Paediatrician”
From the role “Paediatrician” to the role “Physician”; the triangle is at the role “Paediatrician”
From the role “Physician” to the role “Paediatrician”; the triangle is at the role “Physician”
explanation: Specialization runs from the specialised element to the more general one (read as “specializes”), and the hollow triangle is drawn at the target end, i.e. at the more general element. The source is therefore the role “Paediatrician” and the triangle is at the role “Physician”.

image.alt: Overview of the notation of all ArchiMate relationships divided into structural, dependency, dynamic and other, including the AND and OR junctions.

question: How does specialization differ from realization in the notation?
options: Both relationships have a hollow triangle; specialization a solid line, realization a dotted line
Both relationships have a hollow triangle; specialization a dotted line, realization a solid line
Both relationships have a solid line; specialization a hollow triangle, realization an open arrowhead
Both relationships have a dotted line; specialization a hollow triangle, realization a filled arrowhead
explanation: Both relationships end with a hollow triangle at the target and differ in the type of line: specialization is drawn with a solid line, realization with a dotted line. A solid line with an open arrowhead is serving, not realization.

image.alt: Overview of the notation of all ArchiMate relationships divided into structural, dependency, dynamic and other, including the AND and OR junctions.

question: The Application Functions “Identity Verification” and “Credit Check” together, and only together, realize the Application Service “Online Loan Approval”. How is this expressed explicitly?
options: Realization from both functions to an AND junction and from it a realization to the service
Realization from both functions to an OR junction and from it a realization to the service
Two separate realization relationships from the functions to the service, without a junction
Assignment from both functions to an AND junction and from it a realization to the service
explanation: An AND junction explicitly expresses that several elements participate in the relationship together. Two separate realization relationships would be read as each of the functions being able to realize the whole service on its own, and an OR junction as one of them realizing it. A junction moreover connects relationships of the same type, so assignment cannot be combined with realization.

image.alt: Two examples of a junction on a triggering relationship between processes: an AND junction (filled circle) and an OR junction (hollow circle), each with its reading.

question: The Business Process “Goods Receipt” is followed either by the process “Putaway” or by the process “Supplier Complaint”. How is this expressed in ArchiMate?
options: Triggering from the receipt to an OR junction and from it triggering to both processes
Triggering from the receipt to an AND junction and from it triggering to both processes
Triggering from the receipt to an OR junction and from it flow to both processes
Two separate triggering relationships from the receipt to both processes
explanation: An OR junction expresses that one of the connected elements participates in the relationship, i.e. that the goods receipt triggers one of the subsequent processes. An AND junction and two separate triggering relationships would both mean that both processes are triggered. A junction connects relationships of the same type, so triggering cannot be changed to flow through a junction.

image.alt: Two examples of a junction on a triggering relationship between processes: an AND junction (filled circle) and an OR junction (hollow circle), each with its reading.

question: How does the metamodel of motivation elements define the influence relationship?
options: It is defined for the abstract Motivation Element, and so may run between any motivation elements
It is defined from Requirement to Goal, and between other motivation elements it is replaced by association
It is defined between elements of the same type, whereas realization is used between elements of different types
It is defined from Assessment to Driver and is not allowed for other pairs of motivation elements
explanation: In the metamodel, influence is drawn as a relationship of the abstract Motivation Element to itself, so it is inherited by all motivation elements – a goal can influence a driver, a requirement a principle, and also another requirement. The metamodel contains no restriction to a single pair of types or to elements of the same type.

image.alt: Motivation elements and their relationships: stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome, principle, requirement, constraint, meaning and value.

question: Complete: The metamodel of motivation elements draws associations of the Assessment element with two elements, namely ___.
options: Driver and Goal
Stakeholder and Value
Outcome and Principle
Requirement and Meaning
explanation: An assessment is the result of an analysis of the state of the enterprise with respect to a certain driver, so it is associated with the Driver element; the second association leads to the Goal element, with which the organisation responds to the finding. In the metamodel, a Stakeholder is associated with the Driver, Value and Meaning elements, not with the Assessment element.

image.alt: Motivation elements and their relationships: stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome, principle, requirement, constraint, meaning and value.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the metamodel of motivation elements are true?
1. A Stakeholder is associated with the Driver element.
2. A realization relationship runs from the Assessment element to the Driver element.
3. A Value is associated with the Stakeholder and Outcome elements.
4. A Meaning is a specialization of the Value element.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
explanation: The metamodel draws an association between the Stakeholder and Driver elements and associations of the Value element with the Stakeholder and Outcome elements – different stakeholders may attach different value to the same outcome. An assessment is associated with a driver, no realization runs between them, and both Meaning and Value are separate motivation elements without a specialization between them.

image.alt: Motivation elements and their relationships: stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome, principle, requirement, constraint, meaning and value.

question: Which sequence corresponds to the chain of realization relationships in the metamodel of motivation elements, from the most concrete element to the most abstract?
options: Requirement → Principle → Outcome → Goal
Goal → Outcome → Principle → Requirement
Principle → Requirement → Goal → Outcome
Requirement → Outcome → Principle → Goal
explanation: According to the metamodel, realization runs from Requirement to Principle (and also directly to Outcome), from Principle to Outcome and from Outcome to Goal. The opposite direction does not hold: realization does not run from the more abstract goal to more concrete elements, nor from Outcome to Principle.

image.alt: Motivation elements and their relationships: stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome, principle, requirement, constraint, meaning and value.

question: In what way do stakeholders, according to ArchiMate, pursue their interests and concerns with respect to the organisation and its architecture?
options: They set, change and emphasise goals
They perform processes that realize services
They approve deliverables and project milestones
They realize the requirements placed on the solution
explanation: A stakeholder has interests and concerns regarding the organisation and its architecture; to direct effort towards them, it sets, changes and emphasises goals. Performing processes is a matter of the active structure of the core (actors and roles), and requirements are realized by elements of the solution, not by the Stakeholder motivation element.

question: An assessment can reveal strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Which of them are internal to the organisation?
options: Strengths and weaknesses
Opportunities and threats
Strengths and opportunities
Weaknesses and threats
explanation: Strengths and weaknesses describe the organisation itself, so they are internal. Opportunities and threats come from its environment and are therefore external – as are external drivers such as changes in legislation or the economy.

question: Which motivation elements express the required properties of a solution, i.e. the “means” by which goals are achieved?
options: Principle and Requirement
Stakeholder and Assessment
Goal and Outcome
Driver and Meaning
explanation: A Goal represents a desired result (ends), whereas Principle and Requirement describe the properties a solution should have in order to fulfil the goals (means). Goal and Outcome, on the other hand, are results that are being aimed for, and Stakeholder, Driver, Assessment or Meaning do not describe properties of a solution at all.

question: How should an Outcome be named according to the ArchiMate 3.2 recommendations?
options: With a noun and a past-tense verb or adjective, e.g. “Waiting time reduced”
With an infinitive verb and a noun in the active form, e.g. “Reduce waiting time”
With a noun alone and no further specification, e.g. “Waiting time in the outpatient clinic”
With a short sentence formulating a need, e.g. “The system will allow patients to book online”
explanation: The name of an outcome should contain a noun denoting the result and a past-tense verb or an adjective stating that the result has been achieved. The active verb–noun form is recommended for a value stream, a short sentence for a requirement and a noun alone for a driver or a stakeholder.

question: Which of the following recommendations for naming motivation elements does NOT correspond to ArchiMate 3.2?
options: The name of a driver should be an infinitive verb
The name of a stakeholder should preferably be a noun
The name of a requirement is usually a short, clear sentence
The name of a meaning should be a noun or a noun phrase
explanation: A driver is named with a noun (e.g. “Profitability”), not with a verb. The other recommendations hold: a stakeholder should preferably have a noun, a requirement an easily understandable name, often a short sentence, and a meaning a noun or a noun phrase.

question: Complete: An outcome is a result that the organisation produces by its ___; the core elements that realize them participate in it indirectly.
options: capabilities
drivers
assessments
stakeholders
explanation: An outcome is an end result that the organisation produces through its capabilities, and thereby indirectly through the core elements that realize those capabilities. A driver is a condition motivating change, an assessment the result of its analysis and a stakeholder the one who has an interest in the results – none of them produces results.

question: How does a Constraint differ from an ordinary Requirement?
options: It does not prescribe the intended functionality of a system but restricts the way it is realized or how it operates
It applies generally to systems in a given context, whereas a requirement applies to one system
It expresses the result of an analysis of the state of the enterprise with respect to a driver, not a need
It describes the desired end state of the organisation, whereas a requirement describes a means to it
explanation: A constraint is a specialization of a requirement that does not say what the system should be able to do but restricts how it may be realized – it is a restriction on the implementation of the system, on the implementation process or on the operation of the system (e.g. a legal restriction). General validity for systems in a given context belongs to a Principle, and the desired end state is described by a Goal.

image.alt: Ten ArchiMate motivation elements with bevelled corners and icons: Stakeholder, Driver, Assessment, Goal, Outcome, Principle, Requirement, Constraint, Meaning and Value.

question: Which statement about what the Meaning and Value elements can be associated with is consistent with ArchiMate 3.2?
options: Both can be associated with any concept, including core elements
Both can be associated with Business Layer elements, but not with elements of other layers
Meaning is reserved for passive structure, Value for services and products
Both can be associated with a stakeholder, but not with core and strategy elements
explanation: Both Meaning and Value can be associated with any concept: stakeholders may give core elements their own interpretation and attach different value to results. The metamodel of motivation elements explicitly draws only associations with a stakeholder (and, for Value, with an outcome), but no restriction to a layer or aspect follows from that.

question: For the hospital management, the outcome “Waiting time reduced” means cost savings, for patients greater comfort. How should these different benefits be expressed?
options: With two Value elements associated with the outcome and with the respective stakeholder
With two Meaning elements that realize the given outcome for both stakeholders
With two Assessment elements associated with the outcome and with the respective driver
With two Goal elements that the given outcome aggregates for both stakeholders
explanation: Different stakeholders may attach different value to the same outcome; this is expressed by the Value element, which the metamodel associates with the Outcome and Stakeholder elements. Meaning captures the interpretation or knowledge connected with a concept, not its benefit, and an Assessment is the result of an analysis with respect to a driver.

image.alt: Motivation elements and their relationships: stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome, principle, requirement, constraint, meaning and value.

question: In a view of the stakeholders of a city office, the stakeholders “City Council” and “Citizen” are each connected by a solid line without an arrowhead to the same driver “Availability of Services”. What does the view express?
options: The driver is a concern of both stakeholders
The driver is composed of both stakeholders as its parts
Both stakeholders realize the given driver together
The City Council is a specialization of the Citizen stakeholder
explanation: A solid line without an arrowhead is an association; between a stakeholder and a driver it expresses that the driver is a concern of that stakeholder, and the same driver may be shared by several stakeholders. Composition would have a filled diamond at the whole and realization a dotted line with a hollow arrowhead; moreover, the metamodel draws precisely an association between the Stakeholder and Driver elements.

image.alt: Overview of the notation of all ArchiMate relationships divided into structural, dependency, dynamic and other, including the AND and OR junctions.

question: How does a principles view typically connect principles with the goals to which they contribute?
options: With a realization relationship from a principle to a goal; one principle may realize several goals
With a realization relationship from a goal to a principle; one goal may realize several principles
With a specialization relationship from a principle to a goal; a principle is a special kind of goal
With an assignment relationship from a goal to a principle; the goal is assigned to the principle as its owner
explanation: A principle is a means of achieving a goal, so realization runs from the principle to the goal – in the metamodel via Outcome, in the view as a derived direct relationship. The opposite direction does not hold, specialization is allowed between elements of the same type and assignment is not used between motivation elements.

image.alt: Motivation elements and their relationships: stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome, principle, requirement, constraint, meaning and value.

question: The requirement “Patient booking runs through a single portal” fulfils the principle “One point of contact for the patient” and at the same time strongly supports the principle “Digital channel takes precedence” without fulfilling it on its own. With which relationships, drawn from the requirement to these principles, can this be expressed?
options: Realization to the first principle and influence labelled ++ to the second
Influence labelled ++ to the first principle and realization to the second
Aggregation to the first principle and association labelled ++ to the second
Realization to both principles and, for the second, additionally the label ++
explanation: A requirement that fulfils a principle realizes it (realization from the requirement to the principle). A contribution that is not sufficient on its own for fulfilment is expressed by influence, whose strength can be labelled, e.g. ++. The signs belong to influence, not to realization or association, and aggregation in the motivation metamodel is intended for elements of the same type.

question: An element with bevelled corners has, in the top right corner, an icon of a target with an arrow stuck in it. Which element is it?
options: Outcome
Goal
Course of Action
Driver
explanation: A target with an arrow stuck in it denotes an Outcome – a result that has been achieved. A Goal has the target alone, a Driver a ship's wheel, and a Course of Action a target with an arrow that is only heading towards it; moreover, as a behaviour element it has rounded rather than bevelled corners.

image.alt: Ten ArchiMate motivation elements with bevelled corners and icons: Stakeholder, Driver, Assessment, Goal, Outcome, Principle, Requirement, Constraint, Meaning and Value.

question: Which assignment of an icon to a motivation element is correct in the ArchiMate 3.2 notation?
options: Magnifying glass – Assessment
Ship's wheel – Stakeholder
Cloud – Value
Ellipse – Meaning
explanation: Assessment has the magnifying glass icon. The ship's wheel belongs to the Driver element, the cloud (thought bubble) to Meaning and the ellipse to Value; a Stakeholder is marked with a horizontal cylinder.

image.alt: Ten ArchiMate motivation elements with bevelled corners and icons: Stakeholder, Driver, Assessment, Goal, Outcome, Principle, Requirement, Constraint, Meaning and Value.

question: Complete: According to the metamodel of strategy elements, a Resource is an element of ___, whereas Capability, Value Stream and Course of Action are elements of ___.
options: structure; behaviour
behaviour; structure
motivation; behaviour
structure; motivation
explanation: Resource is the only structure element of the strategy layer and is therefore drawn with square corners. Capability and Value Stream (collectively strategy behavior elements) and Course of Action are behaviour elements with rounded corners; none of them is a motivation element.

image.alt: Four ArchiMate strategy elements with icons: Resource, Capability, Value Stream and Course of Action.

question: An e-shop wants to express that the stage “Deliver the parcel” of its value stream is provided by the resource “Network of pick-up points”. Which relationship does the metamodel of strategy elements offer for this?
options: Assignment from the resource to the value stream
Realization from the resource to the value stream
Assignment from the value stream to the resource
Composition from the value stream to the resource
explanation: The metamodel draws assignment from Resource to the abstract Strategy Behavior Element, whose specializations are Capability and Value Stream – a resource can therefore also be assigned to a value stream or its stage. The opposite direction does not hold and a resource is not a part of a value stream; realization runs to a value stream from core behaviour elements, e.g. from business processes.

question:
Which two of the following statements about the metamodel of strategy elements are true?
1. A Course of Action is a structure element to which capabilities are assigned.
2. A Capability can serve (serving) a Course of Action element.
3. A Resource is a specialization of the Capability element.
4. Triggering or flow can run between two capabilities.
options: 2 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
3 and 4
explanation: Strategy behavior elements (capability, value stream) can serve and also realize a Course of Action element, and among themselves they can have triggering, flow and serving relationships. A Course of Action is a behaviour element, not a structure element, and a Resource is a separate structure element that is assigned to a capability, not its specialization.

question: By which core elements is a Resource realized according to ArchiMate 3.2?
options: By active and passive structure elements, e.g. a Business Actor or a Data Object
By internal and external behaviour elements, e.g. a Business Process or a Business Service
By passive structure elements of the application layer, i.e. Data Objects, and by no others
By behaviour elements of the technology layer, e.g. a Technology Process or a Technology Service
explanation: A Resource is realized by active and passive structure elements of the core – for example a Business Actor (a team with a certain competence), an Application Component, Equipment or data elements. From internal and external behaviour elements of the core, realization runs to capabilities and value streams, not to resources.

image.alt: Strategy elements and relationships: a resource assigned to a capability, a capability serves a value stream, strategy elements realize a course of action, which realizes an outcome, and core elements realize strategy elements.

question: Can a Capability be realized (realization) by a Business Service element?
options: Yes, a capability can be realized by internal and external behaviour elements of the core
No, a capability is realized by Business Function elements and services serve it via the serving relationship
No, a service is external behaviour and that does not relate to strategy elements
Yes, but realization runs in the opposite direction, i.e. from the capability to the service
explanation: According to the metamodel of the relationships of strategy elements to core elements, strategy behavior elements (capability, value stream) are realized by internal and external behaviour elements of the core, i.e. by processes and functions as well as services. Realization runs from the more concrete core element to the more abstract capability, not the other way round.

image.alt: Strategy elements and relationships: a resource assigned to a capability, a capability serves a value stream, strategy elements realize a course of action, which realizes an outcome, and core elements realize strategy elements.

question: Which statement about the Resource element is consistent with ArchiMate 3.2?
options: Together with capabilities it is usually a source of competitive advantage, and its strengths and weaknesses are assessed
It is a behaviour element that emphasises what an organisation does, not how it does it
It represents a plan for how to arrange the capabilities of an enterprise to achieve a goal
It is a sequence of activities that create an overall result for a customer
explanation: A Resource is an asset owned or controlled by an individual or an organisation; together with capabilities it is regarded as a source of competitive advantage, it is analysed in terms of strengths and weaknesses and it is taken into account when realizing strategies. The emphasis on “what we do” belongs to Capability, a plan for arranging capabilities and resources is a Course of Action, and a sequence of activities creating a result is a Value Stream.

question: What does a capability map show?
