options: It has a defined start and end, whereas a process is performed on an ongoing basis
It is an active structure element, whereas a process is among the behaviour elements
It has no defined time or resources, whereas a process has them fixed
It is instantaneous and has no duration, whereas a process takes place over time
explanation: A work package is a series of actions that is to deliver specific results in a specified time and with defined resources; it typically has a start and an end, unlike a process that is performed on an ongoing basis. Both a work package and a process are behaviour elements. It is the implementation event, not the work package, that is instantaneous and has no duration.

question: An insurance company manages the programme “Claims handling digitalisation”, which comprises three projects. How should the programme and its projects be modelled in ArchiMate?
options: The programme as a work package and the projects as work packages that the programme aggregates
The programme as a plateau and the projects as work packages that the plateau aggregates
The programme as a grouping and the projects as deliverables that the grouping composes
The programme as a work package and the projects as implementation events inside it
explanation: A work package element can model tasks and sub-projects, whole projects, programmes and project portfolios. Every element may have aggregation and composition with an element of the same type, so a programme (work package) aggregates or composes its projects (work packages). A plateau is a state of the architecture, a deliverable the result of work and an implementation event an instantaneous state change – none of them represents a project.

question: The result of the work package “Customer service transformation” is to be an organisational change, not software or a document. Can such a result be modelled as a deliverable?
options: Yes, a deliverable can be a result of any kind, including an intangible one
No, intangible results are modelled as a gap between two plateaus
No, a deliverable represents documents, for example reports and studies
Yes, provided it is also captured as a business object in the model
explanation: A deliverable is a precisely defined result of a work package and can be a result of any kind – reports, services, software, physical products, but also intangible results such as an organisational change. A gap describes the difference between two plateaus, not the result of work, and no link to a business object is required.

question: In the migration plan of a city office, the implementation event “Pilot operation started” is drawn next to the work package “Portal pilot operation”. How does this element differ from the work package?
options: It is instantaneous – it has no duration and a time at which it occurs can be specified for it
It is ongoing – it lasts for the whole time that the respective plateau applies
It is passive – it cannot trigger another implementation and migration element
It is structural – it describes who is responsible for the given work package
explanation: An implementation event represents a state change related to implementation or migration; a work package has a start and an end, whereas an event is instantaneous and has no duration. It can have a time attribute that states the moment or moments at which it occurs. It is a behaviour element that can trigger work packages, plateaus and other events, so it is neither passive nor structural.

question: The plateau element supports the Baseline, Transition and Target Architecture states known from the TOGAF ADM. What are Transition Architectures used for?
options: For gradual migration: work can be grouped into managed programmes and the benefit of each stage can be shown
For replacing gap analysis: the differences between the baseline and the target state follow from them by themselves
For describing motivation: they capture the drivers and assessments that lead to the architecture change
For managing operations: they describe the continuously performed processes of administering the target architecture
explanation: Transition architectures divide the path from the baseline to the target state into manageable steps: individual work packages and projects can be grouped into managed portfolios and programmes, and the value of each stage for the business is visible. The differences between states continue to be described by the gap element and the reasons for change are captured by motivation elements, not plateaus.

question: From the plateau “Transition state 1”, triggering leads through an OR junction to two plateaus: “Transition state 2 – in-house development” and “Transition state 2 – purchase of a solution”. What does the model express?
options: Transition state 1 is followed by one of the variants; these are alternative migration paths
Transition state 1 is followed by both variants simultaneously; these are parallel migration branches
Transition state 1 is composed of both variants; this is composition expressed by a connector
A gap exists between the two variants; this is a difference captured by means of a junction
explanation: A junction connects relationships of the same type and an OR junction says that one of the branches applies. In a migration view, triggering through an OR junction therefore expresses alternative transition states, of which one is chosen. The simultaneous occurrence of both branches would be expressed by an AND junction; a gap is a separate element associated with plateaus, not the meaning of a junction.

image.alt: Two examples of a junction on a triggering relationship between processes: an AND junction (filled circle) and an OR junction (hollow circle), each with its reading.

question: A project delivers the deliverable “Deployed reservation system”, which gives rise to the application component “Reservation system”. How should this link be expressed in ArchiMate 3.2?
options: Realization from the deliverable to the application component
Realization from the application component to the deliverable
Assignment from the deliverable to the application component
Triggering from the deliverable to the application component
explanation: A deliverable can realize core elements that come into being through its delivery, so realization runs from the deliverable to the application component; realization can likewise lead from a work package to a core element. The opposite direction would say that the application creates the result of the project. Neither assignment nor triggering can be drawn from a passive structure element such as a deliverable.

question: Which relationships lead from a work package or deliverable to a requirement according to the ArchiMate 3.2 specification?
options: Realization and influence
Aggregation and composition
Assignment and serving
Access and triggering
explanation: Both a work package and a deliverable can realize a requirement or influence it by an influence relationship, i.e. affect the degree to which it is met. Aggregation and composition lead to motivation elements from a plateau, which thus groups the goals, outcomes and requirements valid in the given state of the architecture. Assignment, serving, access and triggering are not used between these elements.

question: An element with rounded corners has, in the top right corner, an icon of a circular arrow (a loop ending in an arrowhead). Which element is it?
options: Work package
Implementation event
Business process
Plateau
explanation: The circular arrow is the icon of a work package, which, as a behaviour element, is drawn with rounded corners. An implementation event has the icon of an event with a notch on the left and a rounded end on the right, and a business process the icon of a straight arrow. A plateau is drawn with sharp corners and an icon of three mutually offset bars.

image.alt: Five ArchiMate implementation and migration elements with icons: Work Package, Deliverable, Implementation Event, Plateau and Gap.

question: With which icon is the gap element denoted in ArchiMate 3.2?
options: A circle crossed by two horizontal lines
Three horizontal bars that are offset from one another
A rectangle whose bottom edge is wavy
A circular arrow forming a loop
explanation: A gap has the icon of a circle crossed by two horizontal lines. Three mutually offset horizontal bars denote a plateau, a rectangle with a wavy bottom edge a deliverable and a circular arrow a work package.

image.alt: Five ArchiMate implementation and migration elements with icons: Work Package, Deliverable, Implementation Event, Plateau and Gap.

question: What does an architecture viewpoint prescribe according to its definition?
options: The concepts, models, analysis techniques and visualisations of a view, with the rationale for their choice
The specific elements, relationships and their layout as the architect drew them in the view
The architecture states, work packages, deliverables and gaps needed to achieve a goal
A uniform set of colours, shapes, icons and fonts binding for every diagram in the language
explanation: A viewpoint is a specification of the conventions for a certain kind of view: it determines the perspective from which the view is taken and prescribes the concepts, models, analysis techniques and visualisations that the view provides, together with the rationale for this choice (e.g. a description of the purpose and intended audience). The specific elements and relationships drawn make up only the view itself.

question: A hospital architect has extensive architecture models and is preparing an architecture view for the head of operations. What does such a view consist of?
options: Selected parts of the models that show that his concerns are addressed
Conventions that determine how views of the given kind are created and read
All the models in full, supplemented with a legend of the notation used
A list of his concerns that is written before modelling begins
explanation: A view is a representation of a system from the perspective of a certain set of concerns: it consists of parts of the architecture models selected so as to show the stakeholder that his concerns are addressed. The conventions for a certain kind of view are set by a viewpoint, not a view, and a view neither shows the models in full nor is a mere list of concerns.

question: What is the relationship between the system-of-interest, the architecture and the architecture description in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 conceptual model?
options: The system-of-interest exhibits the architecture and the architecture description expresses it
The architecture description exhibits the architecture and the system-of-interest expresses it
The architecture is a part of the architecture description, like views and viewpoints
The architecture and the architecture description are two names for the same work product
explanation: The system-of-interest exhibits the architecture and the architecture description expresses it – it is a work product that also identifies the system, its stakeholders and their concerns. The architecture itself is therefore neither a document nor a part of the description; the parts of the description are viewpoints, views and the architecture rationale.

image.alt: Conceptual model of an architecture description according to ISO/IEC 42010: stakeholder, concern, system-of-interest, architecture, architecture description, viewpoint, view, model kind and architecture model with labelled relationships.

question: What role does a model kind play in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 conceptual model?
options: It is a part of a viewpoint and governs the architecture models of which a view is composed
It is a part of a view and frames the concerns held by the individual stakeholders
It is a part of an architecture description and expresses the architecture of a system
It is a part of the system-of-interest and identifies its stakeholders
explanation: A viewpoint is composed of one or more model kinds and a view of one or more architecture models; a model kind governs an architecture model in the same way that a viewpoint governs a view. Concerns are framed by the viewpoint as a whole and the architecture of a system is expressed by the architecture description.

image.alt: Conceptual model of an architecture description according to ISO/IEC 42010: stakeholder, concern, system-of-interest, architecture, architecture description, viewpoint, view, model kind and architecture model with labelled relationships.

question: Complete according to the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 conceptual model: An architecture viewpoint ___ concerns, whereas an architecture view ___ them.
options: frames; addresses
addresses; frames
identifies; expresses
governs; exhibits
explanation: In the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 model, a viewpoint frames concerns, i.e. it delimits which concerns views of the given kind deal with, and a view addresses these concerns. They are identified by the architecture description; “governs” is the relationship of a viewpoint to a view and “exhibits” the relationship of a system to its architecture.

image.alt: Conceptual model of an architecture description according to ISO/IEC 42010: stakeholder, concern, system-of-interest, architecture, architecture description, viewpoint, view, model kind and architecture model with labelled relationships.

question:
Which two of the following statements about an architecture description according to ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 are true?
1. It identifies the system-of-interest, its stakeholders and their concerns.
2. It is governed by exactly one model kind.
3. It may contain at most one architecture view.
4. It includes architecture viewpoints, architecture views and architecture rationale.
options: 1 and 4
1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
explanation: An architecture description identifies the system-of-interest, its stakeholders and their concerns and is composed of one or more viewpoints and views, of the architecture rationale and possibly of correspondences and correspondence rules. It can therefore contain several views. A model kind does not govern the architecture description but the architecture models of which views are composed.

image.alt: Conceptual model of an architecture description according to ISO/IEC 42010: stakeholder, concern, system-of-interest, architecture, architecture description, viewpoint, view, model kind and architecture model with labelled relationships.

question: How are a stakeholder, a concern and the system-of-interest related in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 conceptual model?
options: A stakeholder has an interest in the system-of-interest and has one or more concerns
A stakeholder governs the system-of-interest and frames one or more concerns
A concern is a part of the system-of-interest and a stakeholder realizes it
The system-of-interest identifies stakeholders and addresses their concerns
explanation: A stakeholder has interests in the system-of-interest and has concerns; the same concern can be shared by several stakeholders. Stakeholders and concerns are identified by the architecture description, concerns are framed by a viewpoint and addressed by a view – not by the system itself.

image.alt: Conceptual model of an architecture description according to ISO/IEC 42010: stakeholder, concern, system-of-interest, architecture, architecture description, viewpoint, view, model kind and architecture model with labelled relationships.

question: Which values make up the content dimension in the ArchiMate viewpoint classification?
options: Details, Coherence and Overview
Designing, Deciding and Informing
Business, Application and Technology
Structure, Behavior and Motivation
explanation: The viewpoint classification has two dimensions: purpose (Designing, Deciding, Informing) and content (Details, Coherence, Overview), which says what level of detail and what breadth a view offers. Layers and aspects belong to the ArchiMate framework, not to the classification of viewpoints.

image.alt: The two dimensions of the viewpoint classification: purpose (Designing, Deciding, Informing) and content (Details, Coherence, Overview) with typical stakeholders.

question: An architect, a software developer and a business process designer need views that help them find their way around the architecture, design and compare alternatives. Which viewpoint purpose is this?
options: Designing
Deciding
Informing
Details
explanation: The Designing purpose supports architects and designers in navigation, design and design decisions; typical examples are UML and BPMN diagrams, flow charts and ER diagrams. Deciding serves managers' decision-making and Informing explaining and convincing. Details is a value of the content dimension, not of purpose.

image.alt: The two dimensions of the viewpoint classification: purpose (Designing, Deciding, Informing) and content (Details, Coherence, Overview) with typical stakeholders.

question: What are views with the Informing purpose used for and who are they typically intended for?
options: They explain and convince; they are intended for employees, customers and others
They support design and the comparison of alternatives; they are intended for architects and developers
They support investment decisions; they are intended for managers, CIOs and CEOs
They serve the analysis of dependencies and impacts; they are intended for operations managers
explanation: Informing is meant to explain the architecture to employees, customers and other stakeholders, convince them and obtain their commitment; typical forms are animations, cartoons, process illustrations and graphs. Design and the comparison of alternatives belong to the Designing purpose, decision-making to the Deciding purpose and the analysis of dependencies to the Coherence content level.

image.alt: The two dimensions of the viewpoint classification: purpose (Designing, Deciding, Informing) and content (Details, Coherence, Overview) with typical stakeholders.

question: A software engineer designs a single component and a process owner manages a single process; for both, a view of one layer and one aspect suffices, for example a UML class diagram or a BPMN process diagram. Which viewpoint content level is this?
options: Details
Coherence
Overview
Designing
explanation: The Details level is typically limited to one layer and one aspect and serves design and management; typical stakeholders are a software engineer and a process owner. Coherence covers multiple layers or multiple aspects and Overview both. Designing is a value of the purpose dimension, not of content.

image.alt: The two dimensions of the viewpoint classification: purpose (Designing, Deciding, Informing) and content (Details, Coherence, Overview) with typical stakeholders.

question: Who is the Overview content level typically intended for in the viewpoint classification and what does it serve?
options: Enterprise architects, CIOs and CEOs; it serves change management
Software engineers and process owners; it serves design and management (design, manage)
Operations managers; it serves the analysis of dependencies and the impact of changes (impact of change)
Employees and customers; it serves explaining and convincing (explain, convince)
explanation: Overview covers multiple layers and multiple aspects and targets enterprise architects and people with decision-making authority, such as CIOs and CEOs; its purpose is change management. Software engineers and process owners are the typical audience of the Details level and operations managers of the Coherence level. Explaining and convincing belong to the Informing purpose.

image.alt: The two dimensions of the viewpoint classification: purpose (Designing, Deciding, Informing) and content (Details, Coherence, Overview) with typical stakeholders.

question: By which details does the ArchiMate specification characterise an example viewpoint, for example the Organization viewpoint?
options: Stakeholders, concerns, purpose and scope
Drivers, goals, outcomes and requirements
Aspects, layers, elements and relationships
Baseline, transition, target and gap
explanation: The description of an example viewpoint states its typical stakeholders, the concerns it addresses, its purpose (designing, deciding, informing) and its scope, i.e. whether it covers one or several layers and aspects. Aspects, layers, elements and relationships make up the metamodel of the language from which a viewpoint selects; the remaining quartets belong to motivation and to migration.

question: Which concerns does the Organization viewpoint address according to the description in the specification?
options: Identifying competencies, authorities and responsibilities
The consistency and completeness of the structure of data and information
The stability, security and cost of the infrastructure
Dependencies between applications and the orchestration of services
explanation: The Organization viewpoint shows the organisational structure – actors, roles and their placement – and thus helps to identify competencies, authorities and responsibilities. Its scope is one layer and one aspect and it can serve all three purposes: designing, deciding and informing. The other concerns relate to data, infrastructure and the cooperation of applications, i.e. other viewpoints.
